items.title: GkeCodeExecutor sandbox mode raises TypeError with k8s-agent-sandbox >= 0.3

labels.name: agent engine
labels.description: [Component] This issue is related to Vertex AI Agent Engine

items.body:
## 🔴 Required Information

**Describe the Bug:**
`GkeCodeExecutor(executor_type="sandbox")` raises `TypeError` on every call with any current `k8s-agent-sandbox` release. `_execute_in_sandbox` still uses the 0.1.x/0.2.x client API (`SandboxClient(template_name=..., gateway_name=..., namespace=...)`, `sandbox.write`, `sandbox.run`). Since 0.3 the client takes a `connection_config`, and since 0.5 sandboxes are claimed from a `SandboxWarmPool` with `create_sandbox(warmpool=...)`. ADK requires `k8s-agent-sandbox>=0.1.1.post3` with no upper bound, so a fresh `pip install google-adk[extensions]` resolves 1.0.8 and sandbox mode cannot work.

**Steps to Reproduce:**
1. `pip install "google-adk[extensions]"` (resolves `k8s-agent-sandbox==1.0.8`)
2. Create `GkeCodeExecutor(executor_type="sandbox")` with any kubeconfig
3. Call `execute_code(...)`

**Expected Behavior:**
The code runs in a sandbox claimed from the cluster's warm pool.

**Observed Behavior:**
```text
TypeError: SandboxClient.__init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'template_name'
```
The error is raised before any request reaches the cluster.

**Environment Details:**

 - ADK Library Version (pip show google-adk): 2.13.0 (main at 12c7bed)
 - Desktop OS: macOS
 - Python Version (python -V): 3.11

**Model Information:**

 - Are you using LiteLLM: N/A (no model involved)
 - Which model is being used: N/A

---

## 🟡 Optional Information

**Regression:**
It worked only while `k8s-agent-sandbox` 0.1.x/0.2.x was the latest release. `mypy` on main already reports it: `Unexpected keyword argument "template_name" for "SandboxClient"`. The unit tests mock `SandboxClient` without a spec, so they don't catch it.

**Additional Context:**
Tracked upstream as kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox#1038. `SandboxClient` signature by release:

| k8s-agent-sandbox | `SandboxClient(...)` | creates a sandbox with |
|---|---|---|
| 0.1.1.post3, 0.2.1 | `template_name, namespace, gateway_name, ...` | the client itself |
| 0.3.x, 0.4.x | `connection_config, ...` | `create_sandbox(template=...)` |
| 0.5.0 – 1.0.8 | `connection_config, ...` | `create_sandbox(warmpool=...)` |

**Minimal Reproduction Code:**
```python
from unittest import mock
from google.adk.code_executors import gke_code_executor as gke
from google.adk.code_executors.code_execution_utils import CodeExecutionInput

with mock.patch.object(gke.config, "load_incluster_config"), \
     mock.patch.object(gke.client, "BatchV1Api"), \
     mock.patch.object(gke.client, "CoreV1Api"):
  executor = gke.GkeCodeExecutor(executor_type="sandbox")
executor.execute_code(mock.MagicMock(), CodeExecutionInput(code='print("hi")'))
```

**How often has this issue occurred?:**

 - Always (100%)

milestone.description:
Every safety promise in AGENTS.md and the README holds in the code: network, secrets, the owner's tap, the publish gate. 6 epics, 58 issues. Oby Gap Map: https://claude.ai/artifact/4XEY1wYkCTEMBRHfauSxty

GitHub project: https://github.com/orgs/obi-ai-bot/projects/1

items.body:
## What

Before every release of Oby for the Mac, and before every Linux archive of obid, the sandbox's escape tests run on that machine and must pass. A macOS update, a kernel or AppArmor update, or a change in obid that opens a hole in the box, or lets an agent plant a git hook that obid then runs outside the box, stops the release instead of shipping in it.

## Why

Oby's promise that agents stay in their box rests on tests that try to break out of it: through a terminal, Apple events, the keychain, `setsid`, links, abstract sockets (`core/crates/obid/tests/sandbox.rs`). Those tests only protect anyone when they run.

Today they run nowhere by default. GitHub Actions doesn't run for this repository (docs/ci.md, "When jobs don't start"), a worker session runs only the tests its own change touches, and `scripts/release.sh` runs `swift test` and MacTests, not obid's tests. A macOS point release that changes how Seatbelt behaves, or a kernel update on tetrix-lab, would ship with nobody having run them. In places Oby's box is tighter than Codex's and Cursor's (it hides the whole home folder, which theirs don't). Keeping that lead means running its tests on each kind of machine it ships for.

## Today

- **The escape tests** (obid, Rust) in `core/crates/obid/tests/sandbox.rs`:
  - on both systems: `the_check_is_fenced_in_and_has_no_network` (`:482`), `an_agent_is_fenced_in_but_keeps_the_network` (`:492`), `a_committing_job_commits_without_writing_the_clone` (`:508`), `a_job_cannot_reach_the_terminal_obid_was_started_from` (`:585`). The fences they check include the clone's hooks, config and refs, and the worktree's `.git` pointer (`the_same_fences`, `:388`);
  - macOS: `:612`, `:719`, `:905`, `:1096`; Linux: `:1163`, `:1266`, `:1353`.
  - The plug-in box has its own: `core/crates/obi-plugin-host/tests/sandbox.rs`, `macos_services.rs`, and the sandbox cases in `lifecycle.rs`.
- **They can't pass by skipping, mostly.** obid's fail when the box can't be made (`run`, [core/crates/obi-plugin-host/tests/sandbox.rs:305-307](https://github.com/obi-ai-bot/obi/blob/bbcbc1f1b25cfe2357e99090dddd23192182f125/core/crates/obi-plugin-host/tests/sandbox.rs#L305-L307)). The plug-in host's skip unless `OBI_PLUGIN_HOST_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1` ([core/crates/obi-plugin-host/tests/common/mod.rs:15](https://github.com/obi-ai-bot/obi/blob/bbcbc1f1b25cfe2357e99090dddd23192182f125/core/crates/obi-plugin-host/tests/common/mod.rs#L15), `:200-212`).
- **But inside a job's box on macOS** `Sandbox::detect` falls back to the box it inherited (`Tool::Enclosing`, [core/crates/obid/src/sandbox.rs:231-239](https://github.com/obi-ai-bot/obi/blob/bbcbc1f1b25cfe2357e99090dddd23192182f125/core/crates/obid/src/sandbox.rs#L231-L239)). There the tests test the job's box, not the one obid makes.
- **Git.** obid runs every git command with `core.hooksPath=/dev/null`, `core.fsmonitor=false` and `protocol.ext.allow=never` ([core/crates/obid/src/git.rs:24-33](https://github.com/obi-ai-bot/obi/blob/bbcbc1f1b25cfe2357e99090dddd23192182f125/core/crates/obid/src/git.rs#L24-L33)). From the box, the worktree's `.git`, `commondir` and `gitdir` can't be written ([core/crates/obid/src/sandbox.rs:682-697](https://github.com/obi-ai-bot/obi/blob/bbcbc1f1b25cfe2357e99090dddd23192182f125/core/crates/obid/src/sandbox.rs#L682-L697)), and obid takes the job's commits into its own clone itself (`keep_commits`, [core/crates/obid/src/jobs.rs:3491-3543](https://github.com/obi-ai-bot/obi/blob/bbcbc1f1b25cfe2357e99090dddd23192182f125/core/crates/obid/src/jobs.rs#L3491-L3543)). No test plants a hook or a git setting in what a job can write (its worktree, the worktree's own git folder) and then checks that obid's own git never runs it.
- **The release.** `scripts/release.sh` runs two suites in its first step, `swift-test` and `mac-tests` (`:339`), through `scripts/tested.sh`: its suites (`:9`, `:87`), what a record depends on (`tested_paths`, `:26-33`), and the toolchain a record names (`:37-39`: Xcode, Swift and Rust, not the macOS version). docs/release.md, "A release", step 0, says the same.
- **Linux.** `install/package.sh` builds the archive on the machine it is for (`:8`) and runs no test.

## How

**A `sandbox` suite in `scripts/tested.sh`:**

- Its command, in `core/`, with the release's cargo target (`$cache/cargo`), all with `OBI_PLUGIN_HOST_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1 OBID_REQUIRE_OWN_SANDBOX=1`:
  - `cargo test --locked -p obid --test sandbox`;
  - `cargo test --locked -p obid --test jobs_api -- a_hook_or_setting_a_job_plants`;
  - `cargo test --locked -p obi-plugin-host --test sandbox --test macos_services --test lifecycle`.
- Its paths: `core/Cargo.toml`, `core/Cargo.lock`, `core/crates/obid`, `core/crates/obi-plugin-host` and `core/crates/obi-plugin-api`.
- Its record also holds the macOS version and build (`sw_vers -productVersion`, `sw_vers -buildVersion`), so a macOS update runs it again even when no file changed. The other suites' toolchain stays as it is, since their build caches are keyed by it.

**`OBID_REQUIRE_OWN_SANDBOX=1`:** with it, `Sandbox::detect` treats `Tool::Enclosing` as a failure ("obid runs inside another sandbox here, so these tests can't test its own"). A release run from inside a job then never passes without testing anything. Only tests set it, as with `OBID_SECURITY_BIN` (docs/runner-api.md, `claudeKeychain`).

**`scripts/release.sh`:** step 0 runs `sandbox` beside `swift-test` and `mac-tests` (`:339`), skipped only when `tested.sh check sandbox` verifies, and `--full` runs it. The merge ritual can record it with `scripts/tested.sh run sandbox` when a merge changes `core/`.

**Linux, `install/package.sh`:** before it builds the archive it runs the same tests (without `macos_services`), prints `uname -r` and `bwrap --version`, and makes no archive or `.sha256` when one fails. There is no option to skip them.

**A new test for the git side,** `a_hook_or_setting_a_job_plants_never_runs_outside_its_box`, in `core/crates/obid/tests/jobs_api.rs`, with a new task for `tests/agents/fake-claude` (`PLANT-GIT:`):
- inside its box, the agent writes what it can for git to run later: a `config.worktree` in the worktree's own git folder with `core.hooksPath` (pointing at a `.githooks/` folder it fills), `core.fsmonitor`, and a `filter.x.clean` driver that a committed `.gitattributes` names;
- it tries what it can't: the clone's `hooks/`, `config` and `info/attributes`, and the worktree's `.git` pointer;
- then it commits, and obid keeps the commits and publishes (the test's fake `gh`, `tests/agents/gh`);
- each planted program would make a marker file outside the box. None exists.

docs/release.md (step 0, and "Tests a release skips") and docs/install.md (the archive) change in the same pull request.

## Out of scope

- Prompt-injection runs against real agents before each release: #1066.
- A self-check when obid starts, to catch an OS update between releases: not planned here.
- The security review of pull requests: #369.

## Rules this work keeps

- Nothing goes out unless the checks passed and the secret scan is clean. A release is the biggest thing that goes out: it now also waits on the box's tests.
- Agents never hold a code-host login, and vault secrets never reach agents: these are the tests that show it, on each kind of machine Oby ships for.
- The Swift engine (`Engine/`, `Runner/`) is frozen, so this goes into obid (`core/`) and the release scripts. The release keeps running `swift test` as it does now.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `scripts/release.sh <version> --dry-run` runs the `sandbox` suite, and stops before the archive when one of its tests fails (tried once by breaking a fence on a scratch branch).
- [ ] A second release on the same files and the same macOS skips it, saying why; after a macOS update it runs again.
- [ ] Run from inside a job's box, the suite fails, saying obid can't test its own box there.
- [ ] `sh install/package.sh` on Linux runs the tests and makes no archive when one fails.
- [ ] `a_hook_or_setting_a_job_plants_never_runs_outside_its_box` passes on macOS and Linux, and fails when obid's git loses `core.hooksPath=/dev/null` (tried once on a scratch branch).

### Tests and checks

- `core/crates/obid/tests/jobs_api.rs`: `a_hook_or_setting_a_job_plants_never_runs_outside_its_box`.
- `core/crates/obid/tests/sandbox.rs`: `the_sandbox_tests_refuse_an_enclosing_box` (with `OBID_REQUIRE_OWN_SANDBOX=1`).
- `scripts/tested.sh`, by hand: `scripts/tested.sh run sandbox`, then `scripts/tested.sh check sandbox` on the same clean checkout (verifies), and again after changing a file in `core/crates/obid` (doesn't).
- Before the pull request: `cargo test -p obid --test jobs_api -- a_hook_or_setting` and `cargo test -p obid --test sandbox` on a Mac and on Linux; `scripts/release.sh 0.0.0 --dry-run` on a Mac, its output in the pull request; `sh install/package.sh` on tetrix-lab; `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -p obid --all-targets -- -D warnings`, and `gitleaks` on the diff. GitHub Actions doesn't run for this repository: checks run locally, and the pull request reports the checks actually run and what they printed.

### Test it when it's done

1. On the release Mac, run `scripts/release.sh <next version> --dry-run`. Its "Checks" step lists `sandbox` running, then passed.
2. Run it again with nothing changed. It prints `skipped sandbox: tree … passed it on this Mac at …`.
3. On tetrix-lab, run `sh install/package.sh`. It prints the kernel and bubblewrap versions and the tests' result, then makes the archive.

### Where it lands

`scripts/tested.sh`, `scripts/release.sh`, `install/package.sh`, obid's `sandbox.rs` (one switch for tests) and its tests, docs/release.md, docs/install.md. No app changes. Security review required: it decides what must pass before Oby ships, and touches how the sandbox is detected.

### Working on it

Branch from `dev` and open the pull request into `dev`, with Conventional Commits. Update this issue at every step, in the same turn: `status:in-progress` and the branch name when work starts, `status:in-review` and the PR link when it opens, `status:blocked` and what it waits on. Take the status labels off when it merges, and move it on the Oby Gap Map board (https://github.com/orgs/obi-ai-bot/projects/1).

---

items.title: bwrap sandbox have no escape hatches

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

items.body:
I've previously used codex quite a bit (which also offers a bwrap based sandbox). I enabled it for `dirge` too expecting it to work in a similar way. However it seems like the sandbox is very rigid and it's not possible for the agent to ask for more permissions.

As an example I asked the model to get my WAN IP for which it used curl. As far as I understand, because of the strict `--unshare-all` there is no way for the agent to request additional permissions when operations fail.

I patched dirge to allow network within the bwrap sandbox and  asked my agent to migrate a Python project from `poetry` to `uv`. It could use `websearch` to find information, but it couldn't run `uv lock` as the last step to create the lock file as that requires write access to `~/.cache/uv` where `uv` caches package downloads.

I think it would be nice to allow the agent to request running outside the sandbox and/or additional file-system write permissions/network access for specific tool calls when running with bwrap sandboxing.

items.title: Self-hosting the Kubernetes sandbox plugin: chain of blockers (imageRegistry, runtime image tags, agent-sandbox version, sandbox-cr exec probe)
items.body:
## Summary

Self-hosting the Kubernetes sandbox plugin (`@paperclipai/plugin-kubernetes`) currently hits a chain of blockers that make it impossible to run an agent end-to-end without patching Paperclip or working around it at the cluster level. I got all the way to a live Sandbox pod with the adapter binary present, and still couldn't complete a run. Filing the whole chain because each piece is independently actionable.

**Environment:** self-hosted Paperclip **v2026.831.1** (latest) on k3s (containerd 2.2.3-k3s1, K8s 1.3x), external PostgreSQL, `driver: kubernetes`, `inCluster: true`, adapter `claude_local`. Tried `backend: job` then `backend: sandbox-cr`.

---

## Blocker 1 — `imageRegistry` is unusable (server validation vs plugin usage conflict)

The env config `imageRegistry` is validated by the **server** as a URL (zod `.url()` → `{ validation: "url", code: "invalid_string" }`), but the **plugin** (`rewriteRegistry` in `image-allowlist.ts`) uses it as a *bare* registry prefix (`${registry}/${imageName}${tag}`). So:

- `https://ghcr.io/myorg` → passes server validation, but produces the invalid image ref `https://ghcr.io/myorg/agent-runtime-claude:v1` → pod `InvalidImageName`.
- `ghcr.io/myorg` → produces a valid image ref, but the server rejects it: **`Invalid url` on `imageRegistry`**.

**There is no value that satisfies both.** Additionally, `target.imageOverride` (the other documented override, gated by `imageAllowList`) appears **not wired through the server** — 0 references to `imageOverride` under `server/`, so it can never be set for a run. Net: there is no in-app way to point the plugin at a self-hosted runtime image.

**Fix:** either strip the scheme in `rewriteRegistry` (and relax the server zod to accept a bare `host[:port]/path`), or wire `target.imageOverride` end-to-end.

## Blocker 2 — no usable default runtime image tag for self-hosters

`adapter-defaults.ts` hard-codes `ghcr.io/paperclipai/agent-runtime-<adapter>:v1`, but the **public** `ghcr.io/paperclipai/agent-runtime-*` packages publish **only `git-<sha>` tags** — there is no `:v1` (that tag appears to exist only in the hosted service's registry). So a self-host install pulls `...:v1` → `ImagePullBackOff: not found`.

Worse, the latest **agent-runtime-images** build is `git-38d8f37…` (2026-08-21), which **predates the server release** v2026.831.1 (2026-08-31). Combined with Blocker 1, self-hosters have no supported way to get a compatible runtime image.

**Fix:** publish stable/semver runtime image tags to the public registry in lockstep with server releases, and/or document the exact `git-<sha>` to use per server version.

## Blocker 3 — sandbox-cr requires a specific (older) agent-sandbox version; not documented

The plugin emits `apiVersion: agents.x-k8s.io/**v1alpha1**` (`sandbox-cr-builder.ts`), even at HEAD. The current `kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox` release **v1.0.2 serves only `v1beta1`** (v1.0.0 dropped v1alpha1). The newest release that still serves `v1alpha1` is **v0.5.6**. Installing "latest" agent-sandbox silently yields a controller the plugin can't talk to.

**Fix:** either move the plugin to `v1beta1`, or pin/document the compatible agent-sandbox version.

## Blocker 4 — sandbox-cr adapter setup fails to detect the baked-in binary and times out

With everything above worked around (mirrored image → Kyverno rewrite → agent-sandbox v0.5.6 → `backend: sandbox-cr`), a Sandbox pod **does** come up on the correct image, and the adapter binary **is** present:

```
$ kubectl exec <sandbox-pod> -- sh -c 'echo $PATH; command -v claude'
PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin
/usr/bin/claude          # found instantly
```

But the run fails:

```
Timed out while installing the adapter runtime command via:
  if ! command -v 'claude' >/dev/null 2>&1; then ... npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code ... fi
(adapter_failed)   Duration: 8s
```

So Paperclip's own probe (`execution-target.ts`: `command -v <cmd>` via the sandbox exec) does **not** detect `claude`, runs the (multi-minute) install, and times out at ~8s. The recovery recheck (`"if <detectCommand> is on PATH, continuing"`) **also** fails to find it. Since a manual `kubectl exec` finds the binary instantly, the problem is in the **sandbox exec path itself** (`pod-exec.ts` — the `@kubernetes/client-node` WebSocket exec, whose own comments describe a stdin/EOF race). Effectively the exec-based probe/install is unreliable and/or the setup timeout is far too short for the install fallback it triggers.

**Fix:** make the adapter-runtime detection robust in the sandbox exec path (or raise/allow-configuring the setup-command timeout, and don't fall into a minutes-long `npm install` on a fast probe timeout when the binary is already baked into the image).

---

## Net effect

The `job` backend can't run adapters at all (documented: no multi-command exec). The `sandbox-cr` backend is reachable only after (1) building/mirroring a runtime image yourself, (2) working around `imageRegistry` entirely (I used a Kyverno mutating policy to rewrite the image, since no config value works), and (3) pinning agent-sandbox v0.5.6 — and even then Blocker 4 stops the run. Happy to provide more detail / logs on any of these.

items.title: Saving your own command for an agent drops dohc's reply tool, so the agent can't reply

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: local use
labels.description: Affects dohc on one computer, with no sharing or server

items.body:
> [!NOTE]
> 🤖 **Claude Opus 5.5 responding on behalf of Ice**

## For humans

In an agent's settings, you can choose to use your own command. The field fills in the command dohc uses, but that text leaves out the part that lets the agent reply in chat. If you save it, even after changing one thing and changing it back, the agent can no longer reply. Its Check fails with "didn't reply".

The filled-in command should work as it is, or dohc should keep its reply tool when you use your own command.

## Steps

1. Open Settings, then Agents, and pick Claude Code.
2. Choose to use your own command. The field fills in dohc's command.
3. Change one character, change it back, and save.
4. Run Check. It fails with "didn't reply".

## What we know

At `d8f6b23e9`:

- The filled-in text is `launchCommand` (`apps/desktop/src/agents/agentToolCatalog.ts:68`). It calls `agentProfileArguments` without the arguments that start dohc's reply server (`:56`, used at `:60` for Claude Code and `:61` for Codex), so it affects both.
- Editing the field turns off the tool profile, as the field's note says (`apps/desktop/src/renderer/settings/RunnerSettingsCard.tsx:282`, and `apps/desktop/src/renderer/workbench/AddAgentForm.tsx:186` when adding an agent). The agent then runs as a plain command, with no dohc reply tool.
- In a run on Windows with Claude Code 2.1.310, Claude then tried to reply with the `dohc chat reply` command, and Claude Code denied it, because the filled-in command allows only dohc's reply tool. The run log's "The command line is too long." isn't about the reply. It comes from Claude Code's own check of PowerShell commands, which failed on that computer for every command, even outside dohc.
- With Codex's filled-in command, Check fails on Windows too. Codex's sandbox couldn't start the Microsoft Store PowerShell ("Access is denied"). dohc keeps Codex tile runs away from that folder, but not runs of your own command. Not checked on macOS or Linux.
- On Windows, the filled-in command shows paths with doubled backslashes, because `quoteRunnerToken` (`agentToolCatalog.ts:64`) escapes them.

## How it was found

Screenshots of agent settings with a real Claude Code, on Windows.

items.title: Support running TestSpaces (tst run local+fakes) inside the Kiro Crew sandbox

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: tier:T3
labels.description: Changes an existing user experience; needs a one-pager

labels.name: parked
labels.description: Kept open as a request; not on the current plan

items.body:
### Existing issues

- [x] I searched open issues and this is not already requested.

### Problem

## Summary

TestSpaces integration-test runs (`tst run <coordinate>`, e.g. `local+fakes`)
fail immediately inside a Kiro Crew agent session. The failure is a direct,
by-design collision between two sandboxes: TestSpaces needs the
`unshare(2)` syscall to build its own isolation, and Kiro Crew's agent sandbox
denies `unshare(2)` to protect the user's credentials.

Both behaviors are correct. The goal of this issue is **not** to weaken either
sandbox, but to add a first-class, credential-safe path so Kiro Crew users can
run TestSpaces.

## Reproduction

From a tests package directory inside a Kiro Crew agent session:

```
$ tst run local+fakes
  checking workspace …     ok   [0.0s]
  creating sandbox …       fail [0.0s]
    create namespace (sut.local) (namespace holder failed during setup)
```

Run log (`.testspaces/runs/<id>/logs/sandbox/holder.stderr.log`):

```
sandbox holder: unshare failed
```

The syscall returns `EPERM` ("Operation not permitted"). The run aborts before
building the SUT or executing any test.

Confirmed on the host:
- `/proc/self/status` shows `Seccomp: 2` (filter mode), `Seccomp_filters: 1`,
  `NoNewPrivs: 1`, and an empty capability bounding set (`CapBnd: 0…0`).
- Unprivileged user namespaces are **not** disabled at the kernel level
  (`user.max_user_namespaces = 2147483647`), so the blocker is the seccomp
  filter, not kernel policy.
- Direct `unshare --user`, `--net`, and `--mount` all return
  `unshare failed: Operation not permitted`.

## Why TestSpaces does what it does (motivation)

TestSpaces is an integration-test harness. For a `local+fakes` run it stands up
your **system-under-test (SUT)** and a set of **fakes** (mock downstream
services) on the local machine, then runs the test suite against them. Observed
steps from a passing `run.json`:

- `create namespace (sut.local)` — create an isolated network namespace
- `brazil-build server` + `wait for port 8080` — start the SUT
- `mimeo server --port 41103` — start the fakes server
- `forward 127.0.0.1:2014 -> host loopback`, `forward localhost agents -> mimeo`
  — install forwarders that route the SUT's dependency calls to the fakes
- `brazil-build development-integ-tests` — run the tests
- `destroy namespace` — tear everything down

The `unshare` call creates that **network namespace**, and it is load-bearing
for the harness's core guarantees:

1. **Port isolation / reproducibility.** The SUT binds `localhost:8080` and the
   fakes bind `:41103`. Inside a private network namespace those ports exist
   only within the run, so the test can always claim them even if the host is
   already using them, and two runs can execute side-by-side without colliding.

2. **Redirecting dependency traffic to fakes.** This is the whole point of the
   `fakes` coordinate. The SUT believes it is calling real downstream services,
   but a private net namespace lets TestSpaces install routing/forwarding rules
   ("localhost agents -> mimeo", loopback forwarder) that transparently land
   those calls on the fake server instead of the real network — without touching
   the host's networking.

## Kiro Crew denies `unshare` (the other side)

Kiro Crew runs an LLM agent that executes commands with the user's real
credentials on the user's real machine. Its sandbox hides credential files
(`~/.aws`, `~/.ssh`, signing keys, `~/.netrc`, …) from the agent using bind-mount
masks inside a private user+mount namespace, then installs a seccomp-BPF filter
that denies the namespace-manipulation syscalls:

```
mount, umount2, unshare, setns, pivot_root
```

(x86_64 syscall numbers 165, 166, 272, 308, 155.)

The filter's own documentation states the exact threat:

> Denies mount/umount2/unshare/setns/pivot_root so the sandboxed process cannot
> undo the credential bind-mounts (namespace escape). […] with unshare(2) still
> permitted the child can enter a nested user namespace, hold CAP_SYS_ADMIN over
> a copy of this mount tree, and umount every mask — the exact escape this step
> exists to deny.

So `unshare` is denied specifically because, combined with the mount-mask
design, a nested user namespace would grant `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` and let the agent
`umount` the credential masks. This protection must remain intact for general
agent commands.

Seccomp filters are inherited by all children and cannot be removed, so
`tst run` — spawned by the agent — inherits the filter and its `unshare` is
rejected with `EPERM`.

### Proposed behaviour

Add a way to run TestSpaces from a Kiro Crew session that:

- lets TestSpaces create its network namespace  **and**
- does **not** require the user to set `agent.sandbox='off'` /
  `agent.sandbox_allow_unsandboxed_exec=true` as a workaround

### Alternatives considered

The user can configure `agent.sandbox='off'`; however, that may not be safe and we don't want customers to have to configure things to be able to use TestSpaces.

### Anything else

We've had multiple customers who have tried using TestSpaces with KiroCrew and have run into this issue.

Goal: agents create ad-hoc single-purpose agents with a hard tool ceiling. First user: an abliterated model (vllm/glm-5.3-flash) that must get no write or execute tools.

**Phase 1: `tools` on every spec.** A list of regexes, each matched against the whole tool name; None = everything the agent defines. A tool outside it is never offered (`deny` still offers it and refuses the call). Permission modes still apply inside the ceiling. Agents never change it: control, page and plugin `manage` only.
- native: the worker filters the agent's, aid's and plugin tools before the model sees them; `Hello` reports the rest.
- claude-sdk / claude-tty: `--tools` for built-ins, `--strict-mcp-config` with the allowed MCP tools.
- ACP: no protocol way to restrict tools, so a session with `tools` set is refused (`unsupported`), never ignored.

**Phase 2: ad-hoc native agents.** Model + instructions + tools, no `AgentDefinition` class; tools addressable by name from the catalog (coding tools, aid tools, plugin tools).

**Phase 3: spawn**, on #20. An agent creates such a child; the daemon enforces attenuation: child tools ⊆ parent's, modes no looser, sandbox no weaker, parent link.

items.body:
Related to #5701 and #6021 (tool-side follow-up). This issue is the documentation side of the same failure.

## The documented best practice for large text payloads is file handoff

Every major CLI and agent framework routes large text through a file (or stdin fed from a file), never through a single inline argument:

- GitHub CLI, `gh pr create`: `-F, --body-file <file>` — *"Read body text from file (use "-" to read from standard input)"* ([gh manual](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_pr_create))
- Git, `git commit`: `-F <file>` — *"Take the commit message from \<file\>. Use - to read the message from the standard input."* ([git-commit docs](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-commit))
- Anthropic, agent context engineering: *"Structured note-taking — a technique where the agent regularly writes notes persisted to memory outside of the context window"* ([Effective context engineering for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents))

Coding models are trained on exactly this pattern: long content is written to a file with a write tool, and the payload-carrying command receives a pointer (`--body-file`, `-F`).

## The divergence

The AO reviewer sandbox is deliberately read-only — `Write`/`Edit` are removed from the reviewer's toolset (`reviewerDisallowedTools`, since #5904). So the reviewer **cannot perform the first half of the best practice**: it cannot materialize the file that the `--body-file` / `-F` conventions require. The only sanctioned channel left is the exact anti-pattern those conventions exist to prevent: the entire multi-KB review inlined as one giant single-quoted shell argument (`printf '%s' '<full markdown>' | ao review submit --body -`).

Models trained on the file-handoff pattern predictably reach for it first (`cat > /tmp/… <<'EOF'`), find no write tool, fall back to the giant argument — and for models that cannot emit multi-KB single arguments, collapse into no-op loops (#5701: 300+ consecutive no-op calls; #6021: the `PLACEHOLDER` generation failure). The divergence between what the model was trained to do and what the sandbox allows is the fuel of the eternal loop.

## Request

Document the divergence where the reviewer contract is specified, and treat it as a contract decision worth stating explicitly:

- reviewer docs / the review prompt should state that the standard file-handoff pattern is intentionally unavailable in the reviewer sandbox, and why (read-only reviewer; publication is daemon-owned);
- the intended replacement channel for large bodies should be named in the same place, so neither the model nor a reader of the docs is left to improvise toward the pattern they were trained on;
- cross-link with #6021 so the tool-side fix and the documentation land together.

## Acceptance

The reviewer contract docs state the divergence explicitly (no file handoff, why, and what to use instead), and a model following the documented best practice no longer silently dead-ends.

## Summary

I need a way to run CodeWhale **without any sandbox at all** on my own development machine. The kernel-level Seatbelt sandbox is breaking basic shell commands daily, and I've exhausted every workaround.

## Two Sandbox Layers

CodeWhale has two layers:

1. **Internal sandbox** (`--sandbox-mode`) — controllable via config, I have it set to `danger-full-access`
2. **macOS Seatbelt** — kernel-level, compiled into the binary, **not controllable by any config flag**

Layer 2 is the problem. `danger-full-access` bypasses `sandbox-exec` for child processes, but the main TUI process retains Seatbelt restrictions.

## What's Broken (even with danger-full-access)

| Operation | Blocked by |
|-----------|-----------|
| `open -a TextMate file.md` | Seatbelt |
| `ps aux` | Seatbelt |
| `osascript` | Seatbelt |
| `which rsvg-convert` | PATH stripped |
| `git push` | Intermittent |
| `python3.12 script.py` | Intermittent |
| `echo test > ~/Desktop/file` | Seatbelt |
| `find /opt/homebrew` | PATH/Seatbelt |

## Workarounds Tried (all insufficient)

1. `--sandbox-mode danger-full-access` — only affects internal sandbox, not Seatbelt
2. Per-project `sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"` in config.toml — same
3. Rebuilding from source — sandbox baked into build, same behavior
4. Custom `lbl exec` relay (launchd plist → watcher → relay) — works but requires TCC grants, exact bash paths, single-quoting hacks, and breaks on brew upgrades. A Rube Goldberg machine just to run `which convert`.
5. `tasks gate_run` — inconsistent, works for some commands but not general shell
6. `open.txt` trigger + launchd polling — unreliable

## Request

A true zero-sandbox mode. Options, in order of preference:

1. **`--no-sandbox` CLI flag** that strips Seatbelt at runtime
2. **Separate "dev" build** without the Seatbelt entitlement — I'll sign it myself
3. **Entitlements file I can edit** before building from source, with docs
4. **Sanctioned escape hatch** — e.g., `cw exec --unsandboxed` that spawns outside Seatbelt

I'm on my own machine doing local dev. I'll accept any warning, waiver, or "here be dragons" banner. I just need the assistant to stop fighting me at the kernel level.

## Environment

- macOS 15.x, Apple Silicon (M4 Max)
- CodeWhale 0.9.1
- Config: `danger-full-access`, project trusted
- Homebrew tools at `/opt/homebrew/bin`

items.title: Add a per-run sandbox activity report

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

items.body:
LOG ALL TEH THINGZ©

## Why this might be handy (well to me at least)

We can already see a fair bit of what a sandboxed process gets up to. `--observe` can record file paths and connection attempts; the egress proxy records HTTPS `CONNECT` requests, including the hostname, resolved IP, decision, bytes and duration; denials and syscall audit have their own records too.

The catch is that this evidence is spread across a few files and tools. The observe profile mostly gives us deduplicated lists, while the proxy has its own event log and the sandbox summary is mainly about enforcement. After a run, it takes a bit of joining things up to answer a simple question: “what did this thing try to touch, and what actually happened?”

For 3.2, let’s look at a per-run **sandbox activity report** that brings those signals together. Something along these lines:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    T[Sandboxed process tree] --> O[Observe: file and syscall activity]
    T --> P[Egress proxy: CONNECT and DNS resolution]
    T --> D[Policy events: allowed, denied or failed]
    O --> N[Normalise and join by run, time and process]
    P --> N
    D --> N
    N --> J[Per-run activity event log]
    N --> S[Readable activity summary]
```

The aim is to finish a run and see, in one place, that it read these files, wrote those files, checked these paths, tried these network destinations, and had these actions allowed or blocked. Keep the event detail where it’s useful, and give us a summary that doesn’t need `jq` and a brew on the side to understand.

## What we can show already

- File paths opened for reading or writing, and paths checked with `stat`.
- Network connection attempts seen by observe mode.
- HTTPS proxy `CONNECT` attempts with hostname, port, resolved IP, decision, byte counts and duration.
- Sandbox denials, selected syscall audit events, and the enforcement posture the run actually got.

The current observe profile is deliberately more of a behavioural profile than a timeline: it deduplicates paths and connection targets, and an observed syscall does not always tell us whether the operation succeeded. The report must keep **attempted** separate from **allowed**, **denied**, **failed** and **unknown**. No claiming a file was read just because the process tried to open it.

## The awkward bits

- **DNS:** the proxy resolves a hostname for a `CONNECT` and records the result, but we don’t have a full log of DNS queries with query types and decisions. A dedicated DNS listener could give us that for ordinary DNS, provided the sandbox cannot bypass it. DNS-over-HTTPS is just encrypted HTTPS traffic from the sandbox’s point of view, so its individual lookups stay hidden without deeper inspection. Could be a lot of work but im keen on doing it. 
- **HTTPS methods and paths:** for HTTPS, the proxy sees `CONNECT api.example.com:443` and then relays encrypted TLS bytes. It cannot see whether the client sent `GET /thing` or `POST /thing`. TLS interception could expose the request, but it means installing a RAPTOR CA, handling credentials and breaking clients that pin certificates. That wants a separate, opt-in discussion; no default MITM. Pain in the arse but given how agents are doing stuff, useful maybe?
- **Coverage:** observe mode has a record budget and needs tracing support. The report should say when observation was disabled, degraded or truncated, so an empty list doesn’t get mistaken for “nothing happened”.
- **Integrity and privacy:** paths, hostnames and process details can be sensitive, and the run directory can be writable by the target. Reuse the existing provenance protections, bound the output, and sanitise anything shown in a terminal or report.

## Done means

1. A completed run has one obvious place to inspect sandbox activity, with a human-readable summary and machine-readable events.
2. Events identify their source and include a timestamp, process, action, resource/destination and outcome where the source can establish it.
3. The report distinguishes an attempted operation from a confirmed success, and records unknown outcomes honestly.
4. Existing observe, proxy and denial records are joined without inventing missing detail or counting the same event twice.
5. DNS visibility is described accurately; if a controlled DNS path is added, it records query name/type and decision and blocks direct bypass on the relevant lane.
6. HTTPS reporting shows the CONNECT destination and tunnel result. It does not imply that RAPTOR saw the HTTP method or URL path inside TLS.
7. A clear coverage/completeness indicator calls out disabled, degraded, capped or incomplete observation.
8. Target-written telemetry cannot masquerade as RAPTOR-generated activity; output size is bounded and sensitive values are handled safely.
9. `/scorecard` stays about model reliability. The activity report belongs with the individual run, with a link from the run summary if that’s handy.
10. Tests cover event merging, attempted-versus-confirmed outcomes, duplicate handling, incomplete logs, provenance failures and the rendered summary.

## Things to settle while designing it

- Do we extend `sandbox-summary.json`, or give the activity stream its own `sandbox-activity.jsonl` and `sandbox-activity-summary.json`?
- Can a small run report show the useful story, with the full event stream available when someone wants to dig in?
- Which DNS path can we observe and enforce consistently across Linux and macOS? What do we report for direct DNS attempts that are blocked before the name is visible?
- Which actions can be reported as successful, rather than merely attempted, on each platform?
- What gets redacted from paths, hostnames and command details before the report is displayed or exported?
- Keep TLS inspection out of the initial scope, then decide separately whether an explicit opt-in mode is worth the compatibility and trust trade-offs.

## Pointers

- `core/sandbox/tracer.py` — syscall and observe records
- `core/sandbox/observe_profile.py` — paths and connection targets extracted from observe logs
- `core/sandbox/proxy.py` — per-run HTTPS CONNECT events and hostname resolution
- `core/sandbox/egress_summary.py` — current proxy-event aggregation
- `core/sandbox/triage.py` — joins existing sandbox telemetry for run-end triage
- `docs/sandbox.md` — audit, observe, proxy and per-run summary behaviour
- `core/llm/scorecard/` — existing `/scorecard` model reliability feature

**Context**

We tested every Craft CLI's MCP server as a tool for a coding agent (12 apps, release builds tested 2026-10-12; designcraft 0.6.0 and filmcraft 0.6.0 were one release behind current, and I found no confinement flag in either repo's current source). Folder confinement is the main thing that decides whether an app is safe to hand to an agent, and it differs a lot across the suite:

| Confinement | Apps |
|---|---|
| Read and write roots, opt-in | wordcraft, pdfcraft (`--root`), vectorcraft, effectcraft |
| Refuses absolute paths by default, roots available | photocraft |
| No confinement flag | deckcraft, gridcraft, designcraft (storytold/designcraft#242 requests it), lightcraft, filmcraft, soundcraft, cadcraft |

In the last group, the agent's save/export tools wrote outside the working folder in every app we tried, with no flag that could stop them.

**Proposal**

wordcraft already has a careful, self-contained implementation: `crates/engine/src/file_access.rs` (storytold/wordcraft#769). It follows links, compares by whole path components, keeps read and write access separate, and documents its race window. Moving that into craft-libs (as `craft-automation-roots` or similar) would let the seven apps without confinement adopt the same `--automation-read-root` / `--automation-write-root` flags and semantics, and keep behaviour consistent for anyone wiring several Craft apps into one agent.

Happy to help test it against our harness once it lands.

items.title: Feedback from a first day with Television 1.4.23 and sandboxed OpenClaw agents
items.body:
Hi Stephen, Rupert, Josh — thanks for open-sourcing this. We tried Television 1.4.23 today on a small OpenClaw setup (Ubuntu VPS, five agents, viewer on macOS and iOS over Tailscale). Here is a preliminary assessment: what worked for us, and where we hit friction. All of it is from reading the 1.4.23 npm package and running it; happy to be corrected.

## What we liked

- The package is clean: no install scripts, one runtime dependency, MIT.
- Artifacts as pointers to files plus file watching is a good fit for agents: an agent only writes files, and the view updates itself.
- Markdown artifacts with write-back from the editor are the most useful part for us — in the default configuration they are the way a person's input (e.g. ticking `- [ ]`) reaches the agent. We also noticed an ACP bridge in the package (`TELEVISION_ACP_AGENT`, with an `openclaw` profile) but found no documentation — is it meant to be used yet?
- Sensible defaults: loopback only, token auth on, telemetry opt-out clearly documented.

## Where we hit friction

1. **Agents in a sandbox cannot use `tv`.** Our agents run in bubblewrap with loopback blocked, so every `tv` command fails. Writing files works, but registering channels and artifacts does not. We worked around it with a small timer job outside the sandbox that registers new folders as channels and `.md` files as artifacts. A file-based way to register (a drop folder or a manifest the server watches), or a Unix socket, would make Television usable for sandboxed agents without extra tooling.

2. **The startup message prints the connect URL including the token.** Under `tv serve --persist` that line goes to the systemd journal. Our agents read the journal for diagnosis, so the token ended up in an agent transcript and we rotated it. Could the token be printed only to an interactive terminal, or be left out by default (`tv links` already exists)?

3. **iOS "Add to Home Screen" does not work.** The web client removes `token` from the URL and keeps it in `localStorage`. A home-screen web app on iOS has its own, empty storage and only gets the URL without the token, so it shows "access token required". Safari itself works. A small screen for pasting the token, or keeping the token available to the standalone app, would fix it.

4. **Task checkboxes are not persisted.** `tv-tasks` says so ("Nothing is persisted"), but the onboarding channel "Productivity" shows a checkable to-do list, and a user naturally expects the ticks to stay. Persisting task state (similar to the Markdown write-back), or marking the onboarding list as a static demo, would avoid the surprise.

5. **The main skill tells agents to fetch and follow `install.md`** when the user asks for an install, upgrade or configuration change. In setups where the operator manages these, an agent should not follow a remote document that tells it to change the system; we block this explicitly. It would help to put administration into a separate skill that is not installed by default, or to mark the section as operator-only. The main skill is also large (about 44 KB), and much of it is about the CLI, which file-only agents cannot use.

6. **Small CLI issues.** The focus-directive check scans the whole argv, including option values, so a title or name that equals a focus flag (`--title --focus-artifact`) fails with exit code 1. Separately, global options such as `--home` are also accepted after the subcommand. That makes it hard to allow-list individual subcommands safely, for example in a sandbox exception list.

## Our overall impression so far

The idea is good, and it is well built. For our day-to-day use, the clear value right now is a place where agents can update drafts in place: typography drafts, image selections. For daily overviews it did not beat what we already have (a mail digest plus the native calendar), mainly because in the default setup only Markdown is interactive, and a static HTML page in a browser tab gives much of the same. We will run it for two more weeks with two agents and are happy to report back.

We also have two security-related observations that we would rather send privately. Is there a preferred contact? `SECURITY.md` is missing, and so is private vulnerability reporting.

## Summary

The reviewer harness surface has grown to include many interactive agent TUIs. Two safety properties are not consistently enforced today:

1. **Read-only tool access** — some reviewers launch as "host-trusted" without OS isolation or tool allowlists.
2. **Cancel stops active execution** — the "Cancel review" button must reliably interrupt the reviewer's current turn/operation. The TUI pane itself should remain alive for inspection.

This issue tracks making both properties hold for every reviewer harness.

## Current state

### Read-only access is not enforced for all reviewers

- `backend/internal/adapters/reviewer/kimi/kimi.go:47-82` launches Kimi as an **experimental host-trusted reviewer** with only `--plan` mode. It sets no sandbox, no tool allow/deny list, and no permission policy:
  ```go
  []string{binary, "--plan", "--skills-dir", skillsDir}
  ```
  The adapter itself documents the gap at `kimi.go:20-23`:
  > "experimental host-trusted reviewer: Kimi has no OS isolation; terminal users can invoke shell mode, change Plan mode, open an external editor, or alter configuration"

- The frontend classifies Kimi in the host-trusted bucket (`frontend/src/renderer/components/ReviewerSelect.tsx:13`) and shows a warning, but the daemon does not harden the launch.

- By contrast, other reviewers already enforce read-only behavior:
  - `claudecode` uses `AllowedTools`/`DisallowedTools` lists (`backend/internal/adapters/reviewer/claudecode/claudecode.go:44-66`).
  - `codex` uses `--sandbox read-only` (`backend/internal/adapters/reviewer/codex/codex.go:36-63`).
  - `opencode` injects a deny-by-default permission policy (`backend/internal/adapters/reviewer/opencode/opencode.go:38-94`).

### Cancel behavior is inconsistent across reviewers

- The review cancel contract lives in `backend/internal/ports/reviewer.go:25-56` and supports three modes: `interrupt`, `message`, and `input`.
- The launcher dispatches these in `backend/internal/review/launcher.go:543-615`.
- The expectation is **interrupt active execution while keeping the TUI pane alive** — the pane is preserved for inspection.
- Kimi returns a single `Ctrl-C` interrupt (`backend/internal/adapters/reviewer/kimi/kimi.go:99-106`):
  ```go
  return ports.ReviewCancelSpec{Mode: ports.ReviewCancelInterrupt, Interrupts: 1}, nil
  ```
  The adapter comment notes: *"An idle session requires another confirmation before exiting."* This is fine for TUI exit, but the concern is whether one `Ctrl-C` reliably interrupts an active operation.
- The engine correctly marks runs as cancelled when the interrupt succeeds or the pane is dead (`backend/internal/review/review.go:757-768`), but for some harnesses a single `Ctrl-C` may only be swallowed or may not reliably stop the active turn.

## Per-harness audit

### Read-only tool access

| Harness | Status | Evidence / mechanism | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| `claudecode` | ✅ Enforced | `AllowedTools`/`DisallowedTools` lists, `PermissionModeAuto` (`claudecode.go:38-69`) | — |

| `codex` | `input: Escape` | Likely yes | Codex advertises Escape as the interrupt key. |
| `opencode` | `input: [Escape, Escape]` | Likely yes | Two Escapes per OpenCode's active-turn cancel behavior. |
| `kilocode` | `interrupt: 2` | Likely yes | Two Ctrl-C interrupts. |
| `kiro` | `input: Escape` | Likely yes | Escape is the cancel-stream key. |
| `muse` | `input: Escape` | Likely yes | Escape stops active turn. |
| `pi` | `input: Escape` | Likely yes | Escape cancels the active extension operation. |
| `copilot` | `interrupt: 2` | Likely yes | Two interrupts. |
| `amp` | `interrupt: 2` | Likely yes | Two interrupts. |
| `aider` | `interrupt: 2` | Likely yes | Two interrupts. |
| `auggie` | `interrupt: 2` | Likely yes | Two interrupts. |
| `autohand` | `interrupt: 2` | Likely yes | Two interrupts. |
| `cline` | `interrupt: 2` | Likely yes | Two interrupts. |
| `crush` | `interrupt: 2` | Likely yes | Two interrupts. |
| `grok` | `interrupt: 2` | Likely yes | Two interrupts. |
| `agy` | `interrupt: 1` | ⚠️ Possibly insufficient | Adapter comment says first Ctrl-C interrupts active operation, **second begins exit flow**. We only send one, but the risk is that one may not reliably stop active execution in all TUI states. |
| `continueagent` | `input: Escape` | Likely yes | Escape cancels active turn. |
| `devin` | `interrupt: 1` | ⚠️ Possibly insufficient | Only one Ctrl-C; unclear if this reliably stops every active operation. |
| `droid` | `interrupt: 1` | ⚠️ Possibly insufficient | Only one Ctrl-C; unclear if this reliably stops every active operation. |
| `goose` | `interrupt: 1` | ⚠️ Possibly insufficient | Only one Ctrl-C; Goose treats it as active-turn cancellation but robustness across TUI states is untested. |
| `kimi` | `interrupt: 1` | ⚠️ Possibly insufficient | Adapter comment: *"Kimi's documented single Ctrl-C active-operation interrupt."* One interrupt is the documented signal, but should be verified against active tool calls. |
| `qwen` | `input: Escape` | Likely yes | Escape aborts active turn. |
| `vibe` | `input: Escape` | Likely yes | Vibe's native one-Escape interrupt binding. |

### Offenders summary

**Read-only not enforceable (host-trusted):**
`agy`, `continueagent`, `devin`, `droid`, `goose`, `kimi`, `qwen`, `vibe`.

**Cancel signal may not reliably stop active execution:**
`agy`, `devin`, `droid`, `goose`, `kimi` — these use a single interrupt and should be verified/updated to match the harness's documented active-turn cancel behavior.

## Expected behavior

1. **Every reviewer harness launches in a read-only configuration.**
   - No reviewer should be able to write files, commit, push, or mutate the worker checkout unless explicitly allowed by a narrow tool policy.
   - Host-trusted reviewers without native sandbox/policy support should either gain that support or be documented as not meeting the read-only invariant.

2. **Cancel review reliably stops the active execution and returns the reviewer to an idle state. The TUI pane stays alive.**
   - The adapter's `ReviewCancel` spec should send the harness's documented active-turn cancellation signal.
   - The engine should mark `review_run` rows as cancelled once the cancel signal has been delivered, or after confirming the process is no longer executing the review task (or the pane is gone).

## Suggested approach

1. Audit every reviewer adapter under `backend/internal/adapters/reviewer/` and add a per-harness read-only policy analogous to the claude-code/codex/opencode implementations.
2. For Kimi specifically, investigate whether Kimi CLI supports a native read-only/sandbox mode or tool allowlist. If not, consider wrapping the launch or moving Kimi out of the default reviewer set until it can satisfy the invariant.
3. For each host-trusted harness, decide one of:
   - Find and apply a native read-only/sandbox policy.
   - Wrap the harness in a containment layer (OCI / gVisor / minimal sandbox) so the TUI cannot reach the host filesystem.
   - Move the harness out of the default reviewer set and gate it behind an explicit opt-in.
4. Audit each adapter's `ReviewCancel` implementation. For harnesses using a single interrupt (`agy`, `devin`, `droid`, `goose`, `kimi`), verify against the actual CLI that one signal reliably stops active execution. If not, switch to the harness's documented cancel key (Escape, Ctrl-C twice, etc.) or increase the interrupt count.
5. Add launcher/engine tests asserting that cancellation leaves the reviewer in an idle/non-executing state (e.g., probe output for idle prompt) for each harness, without destroying the pane.

## Impact

- **Security/safety:** reviewers are headless and unsupervised; a write-capable reviewer can silently modify the PR under review.
- **User trust:** the "Cancel review" button must reliably stop the active review operation across all reviewers.
- **Scope:** affects all adapters under `backend/internal/adapters/reviewer/`, the launcher (`backend/internal/review/launcher.go`), and the cancel flow in `backend/internal/review/review.go`.

items.body:
## Summary

Since the native-tool permission handler in `src/agents/cli-runner/execute-plugin.ts` was added, every Claude CLI native tool call is gated by the agent's **exec** policy. This includes read-only tools such as `Read` and `ToolSearch`. `resolveCliNativeToolApprovalPlan` (`src/agents/cli-runner/cli-native-tool-approval.ts`) returns:

- `deny` when `security === "deny"`
- `allow` only when `ask === "off"` and `security === "full"`
- `prompt` otherwise

A `claude-cli` agent therefore has three choices:

1. `tools.exec` security `deny`: every native tool is denied, including `Read`. The agent cannot read its own workspace.
2. `full` with ask `off`: every native tool is allowed. Because `tools.deny` is not enforced for claude-cli (#132303, open), `Bash`, `Write` and `Edit` are allowed as well.
3. Ask on: every single `Read` needs an operator approval. When the agent is reached through `sessions_send` from another agent, there may be no approval surface, so the request falls back to deny (`reason: "unavailable"`).

No `mcp__openclaw__read` tool is offered to claude-cli agents, so OpenClaw's own sandboxed read path is not available as a fallback either.

So there is no configuration in which a `claude-cli` agent can **read files but not execute or write**. That is exactly what a code-reviewer agent needs.

## Environment

- OpenClaw 2026.10.5 (1b58cb9), Linux arm64, systemd gateway
- Claude Code 2.1.287, `claude-cli` runtime, model `anthropic/claude-opus-5-5`
- The same logic is present on `main` today (`execute-plugin.ts` around line 211).

## Agent config (relevant part)

```json
{
  "model": "anthropic/claude-opus-5-5",
  "models": { "anthropic/claude-opus-5-5": { "agentRuntime": { "id": "claude-cli" } } },
  "sandbox": { "mode": "all", "backend": "docker", "workspaceAccess": "ro", "scope": "agent" },
  "tools": {
    "deny": ["write", "edit", "apply_patch", "process", "gateway", "message", "secrets", "exec"],
    "exec": { "host": "sandbox", "mode": "deny" }
  }
}
```

## Repro

1. Configure an agent as above.
2. Run `openclaw agent --agent <id> --json -m "Read AGENTS.md in your workspace and reply with its first line."`

**Expected:** the native `Read` works, or OpenClaw offers its own read tool. The agent was intentionally given read-only workspace access, and only exec and write were denied.

**Actual:** `toolSummary: { calls: 2, tools: ["Read"], failures: 2 }`, with this error:

```
PreToolUse:Read hook error: OpenClaw exec policy denied native tool use (security=deny, ask=off).
```

A follow-up turn that tried `ToolSearch` to look for an OpenClaw read tool was denied with the same message. The tools offered under `mcp__openclaw__` were `session_status`, `sessions_history`, `sessions_list`, `sessions_search`, `sessions_send`, `sessions_spawn`, `sessions_yield`, `subagents` and `view_image`. None of them reads text files.

The `executionTrace` confirms the run used `claude-cli` / `claude-opus-5-5` with no fallback. This is not a model-routing problem.

## History

On 2026.9.7 the same agent was blocked by #157126 (MCP bridge scope). That issue was fixed by #165432, and the fix is in 10.5, but the agent is now blocked by this exec gate instead.

## Suggested fix (any one of these)

- Treat read-only native tools (`Read`, `Grep`, `Glob`, `ToolSearch`) separately from exec. Gate them on the agent's `tools.deny` and on sandbox `workspaceAccess`, not on `exec.security`.
- Or honour `tools.allow` and `tools.deny` for native tools (#132303) and pass them to `--tools` / `--disallowedTools`. Then `security: "full"` together with `tools.deny: ["exec","write","edit"]` would give a real read-only agent.
- At minimum, `openclaw doctor` should warn when a claude-cli agent has exec `deny`, because that disables every native tool, including Read.

Related: #132303, #164132, #157126, #165432

items.title: Deny clipboard access by default, with an explicit grant

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

items.body:
### What problem are you trying to solve?

By default, a sandboxed agent can read and write the system clipboard.

This matters in two directions:

1. Read (exfiltration). The clipboard can holds passwords copied from a password manager, 2FA codes, API keys, and session tokens. These are the same secrets nono keeps out of reach on disk and in the keychain. A prompt-injected agent can read the clipboard and send the contents out through any channel it’s allowed, such as an allowed domain, a file in the project, or a commit message.
2. Write (overwriting and poisoning). An agent can replace whatever the user has on the clipboard while they’re working on something else. At best that’s annoying. At worst it’s irreversible, because whatever the user copied, such as a one-off recovery code or a password they haven’t saved yet, is gone. A malicious agent can also put a harmful command on the clipboard. If the user copied benigh code they want to run, but got overwritten and pasted in a terminal outside the sandbox, it runs with full user permissions.

### What would you like to see?

Treat clipboard access as a capability that is denied by default, but can be explicitly granted through:
- **CLI / profile:** a flag such as `--allow-clipboard` and a profile field (e.g. `"clipboard": "allow" | "deny"`). Built-in profiles like `claude-code` should default to deny.
- **Diagnostics:** when clipboard access is denied, `nono` should say so and name the flag that grants it. This avoids users widening the profile blindly.

Some legitimate workflows do need the clipboard, for example, agents that copy generated snippets for the user, so an opt-in rather than a hard deny is preferred.

Possible way of implementation (unverified):
- **macOS:** the base Seatbelt profile currently allows all `mach-lookup` and only denies the keychain services. Adding `(deny mach-lookup (global-name-prefix "com.apple.pasteboard"))` alongside those denies may be enough. A grant would re-allow it through a later rule, the same way authorised keychain access works. Read and write likely can't be split at the Mach service level, so the grant may have to be all-or-nothing on macOS.
- **Linux:** clipboard access goes through the display server, via the Wayland socket in `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` or the X11 sockets (`/tmp/.X11-unix/X*` and the abstract `@/tmp/.X11-unix/X*`). Abstract-socket scoping on Landlock ABI v6+ may already cover the abstract X11 socket. Whether pathname socket connections are blocked needs checking.


### What have you tried instead?

Being more careful with the clipboard while an agent is running in nono, e.g. not copying passwords or codes during a session. It works, but it relies on the user.

### How is this blocking you?

It would be a nice improvement but I have a workaround

### Additional context

Terminal escape sequences such as OSC 52 might let a process set the clipboard by writing to stdout. It might be worth looking into whether nono should account for this.

items.title: Mounts: make some file names read-only for the guest (e.g. .git)
items.body:
### Description

I'm using Lima successfully (great project!!!) with https://github.com/sylvinus/agent-vm to run AI agents in VMs with writable project mounts.

However I have one important outstanding issue: the agent can write `.git/hooks/*` or `.git/config` (e.g. `core.fsmonitor`). Those run on the host the next time I use git in the project, so a malicious agent could actually escape the VM.

Mounting the project read-only isn't an option, since the agent needs to edit the working tree and I want to review/contribute to the diff in real time with my editor of choice.

So I'm proposing a `sshfs.readonlyNames` list for reverse-sshfs mounts:
```
    mountType: "reverse-sshfs"
    mounts:
    - location: "~/my-project"
      writable: true
      sshfs:
        sftpDriver: "builtin"
        readonlyNames: [".git"]
```

Any path with a component matching one of these names is read-only for the guest, at any depth. It is enforced on the host by the builtin SFTP server, so it still holds if the guest is compromised. This needs the builtin server to only serve the mounted directory, which is lima-vm/sshocker#6.

I have a working implementation (sshocker + Lima) and will open PRs. Hoping this can be merged and useful to others!!

## Summary

`designcraft-cli mcp` has no way to confine file access to a folder, so an agent connected to it can read and write anywhere the user can. Please add root flags matching PhotoCraft's `--automation-read-root` / `--automation-write-root`.

## Environment

- DesignCraft: `designcraft-cli 0.4.0` (v0.4.0, windows-x64 portable zip, checksum and signature verified)
- Windows 11 Home, 10.0.26200
- Windows PowerShell 5.1.26100.9549

## Command

```powershell
designcraft-cli.exe mcp --automation-read-root C:\Users\<user>\work --automation-write-root C:\Users\<user>\work
```

## Expected

The server starts and only reads from and writes under the given folder, as PhotoCraft's does.

Exit code 1, nothing on stdout, and on stderr:

```text
designcraft-cli: unknown mcp option `--automation-read-root` (usage: designcraft-cli mcp [--connect PORT] [--sample])
```

The usage line shows the only supported options, so there is currently no sandbox option.

Add root flags to `mcp` that match PhotoCraft's (`--automation-read-root <dir>`, `--automation-write-root <dir>`), so one client config works across the suite. items.title: Planning: execution sandbox boundary for untrusted Agent-generated code
items.body:
# Execution Sandbox Boundary — planning track

Parent mother-platform direction: #137
Related reliability/security hardening: #179
Related Pack/runtime compatibility: #253
Related workspace lifecycle governance: #296
Related agent-aware pre-merge analysis: #298
Historical architecture references: #10, #55, #96

```text
STATUS: PLANNING_ONLY
EXECUTION_AUTHORITY: NONE
ROLE: UNTRUSTED_EXECUTION_ISOLATION_TRACK
STRATEGY: MATURE_SANDBOX_FIRST + LOCAL_FIRST + CAPABILITY_AWARE + FAIL_CLOSED
AUDIT_DATE: 2026-08-22
```

## Why this track exists

The current mother-platform baseline has strong repository/worktree isolation, durable execution, policy/capability checks, secret confinement, evidence verification and trusted publication boundaries. Those controls are necessary but they are **not an operating-system execution sandbox**.

A linked worktree isolates repository mutations; it does not by itself stop Agent-generated or repository-controlled code from reading host files outside the worktree, reaching the network, spawning arbitrary processes, consuming host resources, or interacting with other local state when the concrete executor/tool surface allows it.

The current open roadmap mentions sandbox/container/VM compatibility in Pack requirements (#253) and historically evaluated sandboxed upstream runtimes (#55/#96), but there is no current mother-platform contract that decides **when untrusted execution must cross a stronger sandbox boundary, what guarantees that boundary must provide, how it integrates with TaskStore/Binding/Policy/Evidence, and how the platform behaves when no adequate sandbox is available**.

Contemporary Agent platforms now treat this as commodity infrastructure that should be reused rather than rebuilt. In 2026 GitHub Copilot introduced cloud and local sandboxes restricting Agent shell execution across filesystem/network/system capabilities, while Kubernetes SIG Apps' Agent Sandbox explicitly targets isolated execution of untrusted LLM-generated code and supports stronger runtimes such as gVisor/Kata in cloud deployments.

Primary references:

- https://github.blog/changelog/2026-06-02-cloud-and-local-sandboxes-for-github-copilot-now-in-public-preview/
- https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/03/20/running-agents-on-kubernetes-with-agent-sandbox/
- https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox

## Permanent distinction

```text
Workspace / linked worktree isolation
  = repository mutation and task-workspace separation

Policy / capability boundary
  = what an Agent is authorized to request

Execution sandbox
  = what the operating environment technically permits even if Agent/code is hostile or compromised
```

None substitutes for the others.

Permanent rule:

> Untrusted Agent-generated/repository-controlled execution must not inherit unrestricted trusted-host authority merely because the task itself is approved.

## Scope

Define a provider/executor-neutral isolation contract for execution classes that may run untrusted code, scripts, build hooks, tests, package lifecycle hooks, downloaded/generated binaries or other repository-controlled processes.

The base platform should own only:

```text
isolation requirement classification
sandbox capability contract
policy -> sandbox constraints compilation
sandbox identity/binding in durable run truth
safe input/output/artifact transfer
secret/network/filesystem/resource boundary requirements
observable sandbox lifecycle/result
fail-closed admission when required isolation is unavailable
```

It should **not** build a new container runtime, VM, kernel sandbox or Kubernetes controller.

## Execution isolation classes

A later implementation should define a small closed classification, conceptually:

```text
HOST_TRUSTED
  repository-owned deterministic trusted controller operations only

WORKSPACE_RESTRICTED
  ordinary bounded repository operations where current host/tool policy is sufficient

SANDBOX_REQUIRED
  untrusted generated/repository-controlled code execution requiring stronger filesystem/network/process/resource isolation

SANDBOX_STRONG
  elevated-risk or Pack-defined workloads requiring a stronger backend (for example VM/gVisor/Kata-class isolation where available)
```

Exact names may differ. Classification must be server-owned and cannot be downgraded by task/prompt/model/Pack text.

## Required sandbox capability contract

A sandbox backend/adaptor should declare observable capabilities rather than being represented by a Boolean `sandboxed=true`.

Represent relevant subsets such as:

```text
filesystem_scope
host_home_access
repository_mount_mode
network_mode / endpoint allowlist capability
process/system capability restrictions
resource limits: cpu/memory/pids/disk/time
privilege/root model
nested-container capability
secret injection/reference mechanism
artifact ingress/egress mechanism
snapshot/checkpoint/resume capability
platform/os/architecture
cleanup/disposal guarantees
backend identity/version
```

Task/Pack requirements are matched against these capabilities before execution.

## Local-first backend strategy

Do not require Kubernetes for the current Windows/local-first product.

Evaluate mature backends by environment, for example:

```text
local Windows/macOS/Linux sandbox/runtime mechanisms where reusable
Docker/Podman-compatible isolated runtime where appropriate
existing executor-native sandboxes where their guarantees are inspectable
remote/cloud sandbox adapter when explicitly configured
Kubernetes Agent Sandbox only for deployments where Kubernetes is already justified
stronger gVisor/Kata/VM-class runtime for elevated-risk workloads where supported
```

The platform must not claim equivalent isolation across backends that provide different guarantees.

## Trust and credential boundary

- General GitHub credentials, provider tokens, user-home credential stores and unrelated host secrets must not be mounted into an untrusted sandbox.
- If a task needs a credentialed capability, prefer a trusted host-side broker/relay with scoped lease/reference semantics rather than copying the raw credential into the sandbox.
- Sandbox output is untrusted input to the host until validated/sanitized.
- Sandbox escape, policy mismatch, unexpected privileged capability or uncertain cleanup state is a security failure, not a successful task result.
- A Pack may request a sandbox capability but may not lower the platform's required isolation class or grant itself host access.

## Network boundary

Network behavior must be explicit:

```text
NONE
ALLOWLISTED
BOUNDED_PROXY/BROKER
UNRESTRICTED only under separately justified policy
```

Do not treat ordinary container NAT as a network security policy.

Where package installation/build workflows require network access, compile explicit endpoint/service capability requirements through the existing server-owned policy boundary.

## Filesystem boundary

At minimum distinguish:

```text
read-only source input
writable task workspace
explicit artifact output
host-internal trusted state
user home / credentials
other task workspaces
```

The sandbox must never rely on repository relative paths alone as proof that host access is confined.

## Resource and denial-of-service boundary

Sandbox admission/launch should support bounded limits relevant to unattended operation:

```text
wall-clock timeout
CPU
memory
process/PID count
disk/output quota
network budget where measurable
concurrent sandbox count
```

Resource exhaustion must be surfaced as a typed execution outcome and must integrate with existing budget/retry/recovery truth rather than hanging indefinitely.

## Durable identity and evidence

Each sandboxed run should be able to bind durable execution truth to:

```text
sandbox backend + version
isolation profile digest
input/source identity
workspace/task/run identity
network/filesystem/resource policy digest
start/end lifecycle
exit/failure classification
artifact/output digests
cleanup/disposal result
```

Do not persist raw secrets, unrestricted environment dumps or sensitive host paths merely for observability.

Sandbox lifecycle is execution evidence/telemetry; deterministic task acceptance remains owned by the normal verifier/evidence path.

## Relationship to existing tracks

### #179 H4 policy/capabilities

H4 decides whether an action is authorized. This track provides a stronger technical containment boundary for authorized-but-untrusted execution. Sandbox isolation does not replace policy.

### #179 H6 fresh replay

Fresh-environment replay proves reproducibility. A sandbox may be one implementation backend for replay, but replay and isolation are separate properties.

### #253 Packs

Pack manifests may declare isolation/environment requirements. This Issue owns the mother-platform sandbox capability/admission contract rather than a Pack-specific sandbox implementation.

### #296 workspace lifecycle

Workspace retention/cleanup governs repository workspaces. Sandbox lifecycle may bind to a workspace but has independent resource/disposal semantics. Dirty worktree cleanup rules must not be bypassed by sandbox disposal.

### #298 static security analysis

Static analysis may flag unsafe sinks before merge. Runtime sandboxing reduces blast radius when untrusted code still executes. Neither replaces the other.

## Proposed phases

### ISO-0 — current execution-path threat/capability audit

Read-only audit of current executor/tool/process surfaces.

Acceptance:

- classify which current paths can execute repository/model-controlled code;
- distinguish workspace isolation from actual OS/container isolation;
- identify host filesystem/network/process/secret exposure for each path;
- produce a backend capability comparison;
- no dependency/workflow/runtime mutation required.

### ISO-1 — typed isolation requirement + capability contract

Provider-free deterministic contracts only.

Acceptance:

- server-owned isolation classification;
- backend capability descriptors;
- task/Pack compatibility/admission result;
- no prompt/model can downgrade required isolation;
- `SANDBOX_REQUIRED` without a compatible backend fails before execution.

### ISO-2 — first mature local sandbox adapter

Select the smallest mature backend that fits the actual supported local environment after ISO-0 evidence.

Acceptance:

- filesystem escape fixture is blocked;
- network-disabled/allowlisted behavior is proven;
- host secret/home access is unavailable;
- resource limits and timeout are deterministic enough for product use;
- artifacts can cross the boundary through an explicit sanitized path;
- backend absence/degradation is explicit;
- no general GitHub/provider credential enters the sandbox.

### ISO-3 — executor/Pack integration

Route selected risky execution classes through the sandbox contract while preserving existing TaskStore/Binding/Policy/Evidence authority.

Acceptance:

- trusted controller operations remain outside untrusted sandbox;
- sandboxed executor/tool steps carry exact isolation identity;
- restart/recovery cannot accidentally resume outside the required isolation class;
- Pack isolation requirements compose with platform policy;
- UI/read models can explain `sandbox required / active / blocked / degraded` without pretending all backends are equivalent.

### ISO-4 — optional stronger/remote backend

Only when deployment requirements justify it, add a replaceable stronger backend adapter such as Kubernetes Agent Sandbox/gVisor/Kata/VM-class isolation.

Acceptance:

- backend-specific guarantees remain explicit;
- platform contract stays backend-neutral;
- no Kubernetes dependency is imposed on normal local-first use.

## Deterministic regression matrix

At minimum future implementation/evaluation should cover:

1. generated process tries to read a host-home secret path -> blocked;
2. generated process tries to access another task workspace -> blocked;
3. task requires no network -> outbound network blocked;
4. task requires bounded endpoint -> only authorized route succeeds;
5. subprocess/process bomb -> PID/resource limit terminates or blocks it;
6. disk/output flood -> bounded outcome, no host disk runaway;
7. timeout -> typed terminal/recoverable outcome;
8. sandbox backend unavailable -> required task never silently falls back to unrestricted host execution;
9. malicious sandbox output cannot overwrite trusted control/evidence state directly;
10. raw provider/GitHub credential absent from sandbox env/filesystem/task payload;
11. restart/recovery preserves the required isolation profile;
12. trusted controller Git/GitHub publication remains outside the untrusted sandbox and keeps current authority checks.

## Non-goals

```text
no implementation authority from this Issue
no custom sandbox/container/VM runtime
no mandatory Kubernetes dependency
no claim that Docker alone equals strong isolation
no replacement of TaskStore, LangGraph, Binding, policy or verifier
no automatic credential mounting
no default unrestricted network
no silent host fallback when required isolation is unavailable
no weakening current worktree/path governance
no automatic merge/release/deploy authority
```
